prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B019 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange confirms that no member disputes the science or the maturity. The chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through Holst's human physiology and the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, to Drucker's work on proglucagon-derived peptide biology and receptor actions, is complete. It is followed by large, independently replicated randomised trials showing effects on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. A single part also keeps the three-person limit for the physiology, which is where the discovery lies. A second part would force us to drop one of these names, and I see no candidate on the shortlist whose case is strong enough to justify that this year.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and the committee should record it openly. Habener is outside the credited list yet is plausibly relevant to proglucagon and GLP-1 peptide work. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested and I cannot verify it from the supplied record. The configuration also leaves out Knudsen, whose acylated analogues made the biology into a once-daily or once-weekly drug, so the citation must not read as if the physiology alone delivered the therapy. If the committee cannot accept this attribution risk, I would turn to B014 (June and Sadelain), which is mature and clinically proven but has its own gap in Eshhar and the Rosenberg question. B032 is a further mature alternative, but I now see it as secondary to B014 given the chair's summary that no other member advances it.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps Knudsen as third name, arguing that acylation and albumin binding that turned a minutes-long peptide into a durable drug was a discovery in its own right, and that Mojsov's priority against Habener cannot be adjudicated from the record.
responses.response: I take the first argument seriously and it is the strongest point against my configuration: without half-life extension the physiology would not have reached patients. I still hold that the prize should reward what the hormone is, where it comes from and what it does, because Knudsen's step builds on that and, under a three-person limit, competes with the people who established it. I agree that the priority question cannot be settled from our record, but that argues for a citation worded around the active peptide and physiology, not for removing Mojsov. Mojsov's synthesis and characterisation of GLP-1(7-36) was a necessary step. Your willingness not to block her under a purely physiological citation is what makes the committee's convergence workable. I will not move to Knudsen unless the committee decides the citation must centre on the drug.

responses.point: Perlmann holds that three names understate the chain and that the physiology-to-therapy framing is the cleanest single-part option, with B028 as a two-person fallback if attribution cannot be settled.
responses.response: I agree that the citation is the right place to acknowledge the therapeutic consequence, since the names cannot carry all of it. My wording says the discoveries 'made possible' incretin-based therapies, which credits the physiology without naming industrial development. I also agree that your fallback should be B028 if attribution is judged unsettled, because Walter and Mori have a clean two-name credit. I still rank B014 ahead of B028 as a fallback, because B028 has not yet produced a clinical consequence of comparable weight and I discount discoveries whose medical impact is still indirect. I do not think a documented caveat on Habener and Mojsov justifies deferral, since deferring would not make the record clearer.

responses.point: The chair asks whether a second part is warranted, whether Rosenberg belongs in B014 and how Eshhar's earlier chimeric receptor should be handled, and whether the Habener gap justifies deferring B019 or only a caveat.
responses.response: My answer is that a second part is not warranted this year. The three-person limit applies to the union, so B028 or B014 would cost Holst, Drucker or Mojsov, and I would not weaken the strongest case on the list to add a part that does not clearly outrank the loss. On B014, I agree with you that June and Sadelain carry the CAR design and clinical translation. I would not include Rosenberg, since adoptive cell transfer is framework rather than the CAR discovery, and Eshhar's absence from the credited list is a genuine gap that a citation cannot repair. That is the reason I keep B014 as an alternative and not as a partner. On Habener, a documented caveat is sufficient. The record shows no member claiming the Habener question changes the science, only the names.

responses.point: Sandberg asks whether a second part such as B028 would strengthen or dilute a prize already strong on B019, and worries that omitting drug developers risks citing physiology while the impact came from engineering.
responses.response: I think a second part would dilute it for the reasons above, and B028 in particular would be a prize for a different kind of achievement, a fundamental cell-biological discovery with still-indirect patient impact, awarded at the cost of GLP-1 names. On your engineering concern I disagree in part. The therapeutic impact depended on both physiology and engineering, but the receptor, the active peptide and the human physiology were what made the engineering possible and defined its targets. I do share your caution that the citation should not imply that physiology alone produced the drugs, and I would accept a citation that names the therapy as the consequence.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide relative to Habener can be established from primary sources, which none of us has verified
Whether the committee will accept a physiology-centred citation that leaves Knudsen's acylated analogues as consequence and not credited achievement
If the committee judges the GLP-1 attribution unresolvable, whether B014 without Eshhar is cleaner than B028 or B032
Long-term safety and outcome data for incretin therapies are still accumulating, although I do not treat this as a reason for delay
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, Habener or the June, Sadelain and Rosenberg names. B032 (TNF blockade) lies near my own field of rheumatology, but the profile documents no tie to Feldmann or Maini and I note shared field only. I do not request recusal from any shortlisted ballot.
